passage:
First Monday: Jaya, nineteen, forwarded a video to the family group: a crowd, dramatic music, a caption claiming a whole community had attacked a temple. Within minutes her aunt Hansa replied, "Beta, this is from another country, three years old." Jaya felt her face burn and deleted it.

The next Wednesday: In her college media class, the teacher played the same clip without music. It looked like an ordinary street scuffle. Jaya wrote in her notebook: "Music = telling me what to feel."

Three weeks later: Before sharing anything, she searched for the original source and read at least one article from people she usually disagreed with. Over tea, she told Hansa, "Their argument on the water tax actually made sense. I still don't agree on the rest." Hansa smiled into her cup.

qa.q: How old was the video Jaya forwarded, according to Hansa?
qa.a: It was three years old and from another country.

qa.q: How did Jaya feel when her aunt pointed out the video was fake?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and ashamed, which is why her face burned and she quickly deleted it.

qa.q: Which new habit protects Jaya best, and why?
qa.a: Checking the original source before sharing, because it stops her from spreading misleading clips built to stir emotions.

qa.q: How might Hansa see the change in her niece over those weeks?
qa.a: She seems quietly pleased that Jaya now weighs other views fairly and doesn't just react to dramatic videos.

grounding: Shows over weeks a young adult learning to spot emotional manipulation and misinformation and to consider opposing views fairly.

passage: Sachin set down his tea. "Kamal, before you share that, sit down. Let me tell you about a morning when I was a young reporter in our town. A rumour spread that someone had poisoned the well near the market. By noon people were gathering with sticks, and every version of the story blamed a different family. I was your age, heart pounding, notebook in hand. My editor said, 'Find who saw it. Not who heard it.' I walked to the well. The water had turned cloudy from a broken pipe. That was all. We printed it, and the crowd went home. Since then I've read two newspapers every morning, one I like and one that annoys me. The annoying one keeps me honest. Now, where did your clip come from?"

qa.q: What did Sachin's editor tell him to find?
qa.a: Who saw it, not who heard it.

qa.q: What does Sachin think Kamal might be about to do, and why does that worry him?
qa.a: He thinks Kamal is about to share a clip without checking it, and he worries because he has seen how fast rumours can stir angry crowds.

qa.q: What would Sachin advise Kamal to do with the clip?
qa.a: Trace it back to someone who actually saw the event, and look at other sources, including ones he disagrees with, before sharing.

qa.q: How might the family that was blamed have felt if the rumour hadn't been checked?
qa.a: They could have faced fear and violence for something that never happened, so the checking protected innocent people. 🙏

grounding: An elder tells a young adult how checking facts stopped a dangerous rumour and why he reads opposing views.

passage: Anirban had two hours to submit his assignment: evaluate a viral post claiming a new city law would ban street vendors. The hostel Wi-Fi had died, so he and Santosh squeezed into a noisy cybercafe with a flickering monitor. The post used a crying vendor's photo and bold red letters. Anirban's first reaction was anger. Then he paused. "Why is it so loud?" he muttered. He found the actual draft law on the municipal site. It proposed vending zones, not a ban. He also opened a column from a vendors' union arguing the zones were too far from customers. Their point seemed fair. With twenty minutes left, he wrote: the post was misleading, but the worry behind it deserved a real hearing. Santosh read it over his shoulder. "Balanced, man."

qa.q: What did the actual draft law propose?
qa.a: It proposed vending zones, not a ban.

qa.q: Why did Anirban pause after his first angry reaction?
qa.a: He noticed the post seemed designed to stir emotion, which made him suspicious and want to check.

qa.q: Which part of Anirban's approach was most fair-minded?
qa.a: He checked the real law but still took the vendors' union's concern seriously, instead of dismissing one side.

qa.q: How might a vendor reading Anirban's conclusion feel?
qa.a: They might feel their worry was respected, even though the scary claim of a ban was shown to be false.

grounding: Shows a young adult under time pressure identifying misinformation while fairly weighing an opposing view.

passage: The clip reached Deepika's phone at 10 pm in her PG in Chandigarh: blurry footage of young men smashing a bus stop, captioned 'Students from THAT college did this today!! Share before it's deleted!!' Her floor group was already furious. Deepika, twenty-one, felt her own anger rise; that college had beaten hers in the debate finals. Then she noticed the capital letters, the rush, the 'before it's deleted.' She paused the clip. The shop signs were in a script she didn't recognise, and everyone wore winter coats, in May. She searched a still frame and found the same video from two years ago, in another country. She posted the link in the group. Gurleen replied, 'Okay, but they're still annoying.' Deepika laughed. 'Annoying, sure. Not criminals.'

qa.q: What did the caption tell people to do?
qa.a: Share it before it's deleted.

qa.q: Why did Deepika feel her anger rise at first?
qa.a: The clip targeted a college that had beaten hers in the debate finals, so it fed an existing grudge.

qa.q: Which clues helped Deepika spot that the clip was false?
qa.a: The shouting urgency of the caption, shop signs in an unfamiliar script and winter coats in May, which she then checked by searching a frame.

qa.q: How might students of the accused college be affected if the clip spread?
qa.a: They could be blamed and harassed for something they never did.

grounding: Shows a young adult noticing emotional manipulation in a viral clip and checking it before believing or sharing.

passage:
'Papa, that channel only interviews people who agree with them.'
'And your videos only show people who agree with you.'
Jagdish opened his mouth. Parul, his sister, looked up from her phone. 'He's got you there.'
'Fine. But the metro line will cut traffic by half.'
'Who said half?'
'The... video.'
'And who made the video?'
'...The company building it.' Jagdish rubbed his face. 'Okay. That's not neutral either.'
Papa softened. 'I'm not against the metro, beta. I'm against cutting the old trees in the market without asking anyone.'
'Wait, that's your whole objection?'
'That's what the channel never lets me say.'
Parul laughed. 'So you two agree more than your screens do.'
Jagdish opened the city council's report. 'Let's read the actual plan. Both of us. Tonight.'

qa.q: What is Papa's real objection to the metro line?
qa.a: Cutting the old trees in the market without asking anyone.

qa.q: What did Jagdish realise when he rubbed his face?
qa.a: He felt a bit embarrassed as he realised his own source was biased too, since it came from the company building the line.

qa.q: Why is reading the actual plan together a good next step?
qa.a: It moves them from competing slanted sources to the original document, and they check it together fairly.

qa.q: How does Parul see the argument?
qa.a: She sees that her father and brother agree more than they thought, and the screens made them seem further apart.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult recognising bias in his own sources and hearing an opposing view fairly.
